title: Memory, I/O interfacing and interrupts
subtitle: Connecting real chips to the bus so the processor reaches each one at exactly the right address.

8086.title: 8086 interrupts and the vector table
8086.body: The 8086 supports 256 interrupt types. Type n has a 4-byte entry (IP then CS) at address 4n in the interrupt vector table occupying 0000H–03FFH. Sources: hardware (NMI type 2, INTR with type from the PIC), software (INT n) and exceptions (divide error type 0, single-step type 1, breakpoint type 3, overflow type 4). The 8259 PIC prioritises up to 8 (cascaded, 64) devices.
8086.steps: Where is the vector for interrupt type 21H? Address = 4 × 21H = 84H; the four bytes at 0084H–0087H hold IP then CS of the handler.

decode.title: Address decoding
decode.body: Each memory or I/O chip has a chip-select input; address decoding turns the high address lines into select signals so exactly one chip responds. Full (unique) decoding uses all the high lines, so each location has one address; partial (non-unique) decoding ignores some, so the chip appears at several addresses (simpler hardware). Decoders (74LS138 3-to-8) or NAND gates generate the selects.
decode.steps: An 8 KB RAM (2000H–3FFFH) on an 8085. Which lines select it? 8 KB = 2¹³, so A0–A12 go to the chip. The range 2000H–3FFFH has A15A14A13 = 001.

map.title: Memory-mapped I/O versus I/O-mapped I/O
map.body: In memory-mapped I/O a device lives in the memory address space, so ordinary instructions (MOV, LDA, STA) access it, at the cost of memory addresses. In I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O a separate 256-port space is reached by IN and OUT with the IO/M̅ line high; the memory map stays free.

ppi.title: Parallel interface: the 8255 PPI
ppi.body: The 8255 gives three 8-bit ports (A, B, C) programmed through a control word. Mode 0: simple input/output; Mode 1: strobed I/O with handshake; Mode 2: bidirectional. Handshaking: the device signals “data ready”, the processor reads and acknowledges — needed when the two run at different speeds.
ppi.steps: Program the 8255: port A output, port B input, port C output, Mode 0. Control word: D7 = 1 (mode set), D6–D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 0 (C upper out), D2 = 0, D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out).

serial.title: Serial interface
serial.body: Serial transmission sends bits one after another. Asynchronous: each character is framed by a start bit (0) and stop bit(s) (1) so the receiver re-synchronises every byte; synchronous: a continuous block with a shared clock or sync characters, more efficient. RS-232 defines voltage levels and a 9/25-pin connector; USB is the modern serial bus; the 8251 USART does the conversion. Baud 9600 with 8N1 frames (10 bits/char) moves 960 characters/s.
serial.steps: A link at 9600 baud sends 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1). Bits per character = 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10, so characters per second = 9600/10. Efficiency = 8/10 = 80%.

int.title: Interrupts
int.body: Polling asks the device repeatedly; an interrupt lets the device ask for attention, so the CPU does useful work meanwhile. The 8085 has five hardware interrupts in priority order: TRAP (non-maskable), RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR; each RST has a fixed vector (RST7.5 → 003CH, 6.5 → 0034H, 5.5 → 002CH, TRAP → 0024H). EI/DI enable and disable maskable interrupts; SIM/RIM set and read the masks. Processing: finish the instruction, push PC, jump to the vector, run the service routine, RET/EI.

adv.title: Advanced topics: RISC, CISC, control, DSP
adv.body: Accumulator-based machines (8085) route every result through A; register-based machines (8086 and later) use many registers. Hardwired control is fast; microprogrammed control is flexible. RISC (few simple instructions, pipelined) versus CISC (many complex ones). Multitasking needs protection and memory management support; a digital signal processor adds hardware multiply–accumulate and Harvard buses for real-time filtering.
